[675](#675)    pub fn build(self) -> Result<RouteDefinition, CamelError> {
[681](#681)        validate_uri(&self.from_uri)?;
[682](#682)        let route_id = self
[683](#683)            .route_id
[684](#684)            .filter(|s| !s.trim().is_empty())
[685](#685)            .ok_or_else(|| {
[686](#686)                CamelError::RouteError(
[687](#687)                    "route must have a non-empty 'route_id' — call .route_id(\"name\") on the builder"
[688](#688)                        .to_string(),
[689](#689)                )
[690](#690)            })?;
[691](#691)        let resolved_error_handler = match self.error_handler_mode {
[692](#692)            ErrorHandlerMode::None => self.error_handler,
[693](#693)            ErrorHandlerMode::ExplicitConfig => self.error_handler,
[694](#694)            ErrorHandlerMode::Mixed => {
[695](#695)                return Err(CamelError::RouteError(
[696](#696)                    "mixed error handler modes: cannot combine .error_handler(config) with shorthand methods".into(),
[697](#697)                ));
[698](#698)            }
[699](#699)            ErrorHandlerMode::Shorthand { dlc_uri, specs } => {
[700](#700)                let mut config = if let Some(uri) = dlc_uri {
[701](#701)                    ErrorHandlerConfig::dead_letter_channel(uri)
[702](#702)                } else {
[703](#703)                    ErrorHandlerConfig::log_only()
[704](#704)                };
[705](#705)
[706](#706)                for spec in specs {
[707](#707)                    let matcher = spec.matches.clone();
[708](#708)                    let mut builder = config.on_exception(move |e| matcher(e));
[709](#709)
[710](#710)                    if let Some(retry) = spec.retry {
[711](#711)                        builder = builder.retry(retry.max_attempts).with_backoff(
[712](#712)                            retry.initial_delay,
[713](#713)                            retry.multiplier,
[714](#714)                            retry.max_delay,
[715](#715)                        );
[716](#716)                        if retry.jitter_factor > 0.0 {
[717](#717)                            builder = builder.with_jitter(retry.jitter_factor);
[718](#718)                        }
[719](#719)                    }
[720](#720)
[721](#721)                    if let Some(uri) = spec.handled_by {
[722](#722)                        builder = builder.handled_by(uri);
[723](#723)                    }
[724](#724)
[725](#725)                    config = builder.build();
[726](#726)                }
[727](#727)
[728](#728)                Some(config)
[729](#729)            }
[730](#730)        };
[731](#731)
[732](#732)        let definition = RouteDefinition::new(self.from_uri, self.steps);
[733](#733)        let definition = if let Some(eh) = resolved_error_handler {
[734](#734)            definition.with_error_handler(eh)
[735](#735)        } else {
[736](#736)            definition
[737](#737)        };
[738](#738)        let definition = if let Some(cb) = self.circuit_breaker_config {
[739](#739)            definition.with_circuit_breaker(cb)
[740](#740)        } else {
[741](#741)            definition
[742](#742)        };
[743](#743)        let definition = if let Some(sp) = self.security_policy_config {
[744](#744)            definition.with_security_policy(sp)
[745](#745)        } else {
[746](#746)            definition
[747](#747)        };
[748](#748)        let definition = if let Some(auth) = self.security_authenticator {
[749](#749)            definition.with_security_authenticator(auth)
[750](#750)        } else {
[751](#751)            definition
[752](#752)        };
[753](#753)        let definition = if let Some(concurrency) = self.concurrency {
[754](#754)            definition.with_concurrency(concurrency)
[755](#755)        } else {
[756](#756)            definition
[757](#757)        };
[758](#758)        let definition = definition.with_route_id(route_id);
[759](#759)        let definition = if let Some(auto) = self.auto_startup {
[760](#760)            definition.with_auto_startup(auto)
[761](#761)        } else {
[762](#762)            definition
[763](#763)        };
[764](#764)        let definition = if let Some(order) = self.startup_order {
[765](#765)            definition.with_startup_order(order)
[766](#766)        } else {
[767](#767)            definition
[768](#768)        };
[769](#769)        Ok(definition)
[770](#770)    }
[771](#771)
[772](#772)    pub fn build_canonical(self) -> Result<CanonicalRouteSpec, CamelError> {
[774](#774)        validate_uri(&self.from_uri)?;
[775](#775)        let route_id = self
[776](#776)            .route_id
[777](#777)            .filter(|s| !s.trim().is_empty())
[778](#778)            .ok_or_else(|| {
[779](#779)                CamelError::RouteError(
[780](#780)                    "route must have a non-empty 'route_id' — call .route_id(\"name\") on the builder"
[781](#781)                        .to_string(),
[782](#782)                )
[783](#783)            })?;
[784](#784)
[785](#785)        let steps = canonicalize_steps(self.steps)?;
[786](#786)        let circuit_breaker = self
[787](#787)            .circuit_breaker_config
[788](#788)            .map(canonicalize_circuit_breaker);
[789](#789)
[790](#790)        if self.security_policy_config.is_some() {
[791](#791)            return Err(CamelError::RouteError(
[792](#792)                "routes with security_policy cannot use the canonical/hot-reload path (not yet supported)"
[793](#793)                    .into(),
[794](#794)            ));
[795](#795)        }
[796](#796)
[797](#797)        let spec = CanonicalRouteSpec {
[798](#798)            route_id,
[799](#799)            from: self.from_uri,
[800](#800)            steps,
[801](#801)            circuit_breaker,
[802](#802)            auto_startup: None,
[803](#803)            startup_order: None,
[804](#804)            concurrency: None,
[805](#805)            version: camel_api::CANONICAL_CONTRACT_VERSION,
[806](#806)        };
[807](#807)        spec.validate_contract()?;
[808](#808)        Ok(spec)
[809](#809)    }

[861](#861)fn validate_uri(uri: &str) -> Result<(), CamelError> {
[863](#863)    let trimmed = uri.trim();
[864](#864)    if trimmed.is_empty() {
[865](#865)        return Err(CamelError::RouteError(
[866](#866)            "route must have a 'from' URI".to_string(),
[867](#867)        ));
[868](#868)    }
[869](#869)    if !trimmed.contains(':') {
[870](#870)        return Err(CamelError::RouteError(
[871](#871)            "URI must have a scheme (e.g. 'timer:tick')".to_string(),
[872](#872)        ));
[873](#873)    }
[874](#874)    let scheme = trimmed.split(':').next().unwrap_or("");
[875](#875)    if scheme.trim().is_empty() {
[876](#876)        return Err(CamelError::RouteError(
[877](#877)            "URI scheme must not be empty".to_string(),
[878](#878)        ));
[879](#879)    }
[880](#880)    Ok(())
[881](#881)}

[883](#883)fn canonicalize_steps(steps: Vec<BuilderStep>) -> Result<Vec<CanonicalStepSpec>, CamelError> {
[884](#884)    let mut canonical = Vec::with_capacity(steps.len());
[885](#885)    for step in steps {
[886](#886)        canonical.push(canonicalize_step(step)?);
[887](#887)    }
[888](#888)    Ok(canonical)
[889](#889)}
[890](#890)
[891](#891)fn canonicalize_step(step: BuilderStep) -> Result<CanonicalStepSpec, CamelError> {
[892](#892)    match step {
[893](#893)        BuilderStep::To(uri) => Ok(CanonicalStepSpec::To { uri }),
[894](#894)        BuilderStep::Log { message, .. } => Ok(CanonicalStepSpec::Log { message }),
[895](#895)        BuilderStep::Stop => Ok(CanonicalStepSpec::Stop),
[896](#896)        BuilderStep::WireTap { uri } => Ok(CanonicalStepSpec::WireTap { uri }),
[897](#897)        BuilderStep::Delay { config } => Ok(CanonicalStepSpec::Delay {
[898](#898)            delay_ms: config.delay_ms,
[899](#899)            dynamic_header: config.dynamic_header,
[900](#900)        }),
[901](#901)        BuilderStep::DeclarativeScript { expression } => {
[902](#902)            Ok(CanonicalStepSpec::Script { expression })
[903](#903)        }
[904](#904)        BuilderStep::DeclarativeFilter { predicate, steps } => Ok(CanonicalStepSpec::Filter {
[905](#905)            predicate,
[906](#906)            steps: canonicalize_steps(steps)?,
[907](#907)        }),
[908](#908)        BuilderStep::DeclarativeChoice { whens, otherwise } => {
[909](#909)            let mut canonical_whens = Vec::with_capacity(whens.len());
[910](#910)            for DeclarativeWhenStep { predicate, steps } in whens {
[911](#911)                canonical_whens.push(CanonicalWhenSpec {
[912](#912)                    predicate,
[913](#913)                    steps: canonicalize_steps(steps)?,
[914](#914)                });
[915](#915)            }
[916](#916)            let otherwise = match otherwise {
[917](#917)                Some(steps) => Some(canonicalize_steps(steps)?),
[918](#918)                None => None,
[919](#919)            };
[920](#920)            Ok(CanonicalStepSpec::Choice {
[921](#921)                whens: canonical_whens,
[922](#922)                otherwise,
[923](#923)            })
[924](#924)        }
[925](#925)        BuilderStep::DeclarativeSplit {
[926](#926)            expression,
[927](#927)            aggregation,
[928](#928)            parallel,
[929](#929)            parallel_limit,
[930](#930)            stop_on_exception,
[931](#931)            steps,
[932](#932)        } => Ok(CanonicalStepSpec::Split {
[933](#933)            expression: CanonicalSplitExpressionSpec::Language(expression),
[934](#934)            aggregation: canonicalize_split_aggregation(aggregation)?,
[935](#935)            parallel,
[936](#936)            parallel_limit,
[937](#937)            stop_on_exception,
[938](#938)            steps: canonicalize_steps(steps)?,
[939](#939)        }),
[940](#940)        BuilderStep::Aggregate { config } => Ok(CanonicalStepSpec::Aggregate(
[941](#941)            canonicalize_aggregate(config)?,
[942](#942)        )),
[943](#943)        other => {
[944](#944)            let step_name = canonical_step_name(&other);
[945](#945)            let detail = camel_api::canonical_contract_rejection_reason(step_name)
[946](#946)                .unwrap_or("not included in canonical v1");
[947](#947)            Err(CamelError::RouteError(format!(
[948](#948)                "canonical v1 does not support step `{step_name}`: {detail}"
[949](#949)            )))
[950](#950)        }
[951](#951)    }
[952](#952)}
[953](#953)
[954](#954)fn canonicalize_split_aggregation(
[955](#955)    strategy: camel_api::splitter::AggregationStrategy,
[956](#956)) -> Result<CanonicalSplitAggregationSpec, CamelError> {
[957](#957)    match strategy {
[958](#958)        camel_api::splitter::AggregationStrategy::LastWins => {
[959](#959)            Ok(CanonicalSplitAggregationSpec::LastWins)
[960](#960)        }
[961](#961)        camel_api::splitter::AggregationStrategy::CollectAll => {
[962](#962)            Ok(CanonicalSplitAggregationSpec::CollectAll)
[963](#963)        }
[964](#964)        camel_api::splitter::AggregationStrategy::Custom(_) => Err(CamelError::RouteError(
[965](#965)            "canonical v1 does not support custom split aggregation".to_string(),
[966](#966)        )),
[967](#967)        camel_api::splitter::AggregationStrategy::Original => {
[968](#968)            Ok(CanonicalSplitAggregationSpec::Original)
[969](#969)        }
[970](#970)    }
[971](#971)}
[972](#972)
[973](#973)fn extract_completion_fields(
[974](#974)    mode: &CompletionMode,
[975](#975)) -> Result<(Option<usize>, Option<u64>), CamelError> {
[976](#976)    match mode {
[977](#977)        CompletionMode::Single(cond) => match cond {
[978](#978)            CompletionCondition::Size(n) => Ok((Some(*n), None)),
[979](#979)            CompletionCondition::Timeout(d) => Ok((None, Some(d.as_millis() as u64))),
[980](#980)            CompletionCondition::Predicate(_) => Err(CamelError::RouteError(
[981](#981)                "canonical v1 does not support aggregate predicate completion".to_string(),
[982](#982)            )),
[983](#983)        },
[984](#984)        CompletionMode::Any(conds) => {
[985](#985)            let mut size = None;
[986](#986)            let mut timeout_ms = None;
[987](#987)            for cond in conds {
[988](#988)                match cond {
[989](#989)                    CompletionCondition::Size(n) => size = Some(*n),
[990](#990)                    CompletionCondition::Timeout(d) => timeout_ms = Some(d.as_millis() as u64),
[991](#991)                    CompletionCondition::Predicate(_) => {
[992](#992)                        return Err(CamelError::RouteError(
[993](#993)                            "canonical v1 does not support aggregate predicate completion"
[994](#994)                                .to_string(),
[995](#995)                        ));
[996](#996)                    }
[997](#997)                }
[998](#998)            }
[999](#999)            Ok((size, timeout_ms))
[1000](#1000)        }
[1001](#1001)    }
[1002](#1002)}
[1003](#1003)
[1004](#1004)fn canonicalize_aggregate(config: AggregatorConfig) -> Result<CanonicalAggregateSpec, CamelError> {
[1005](#1005)    let (completion_size, completion_timeout_ms) = extract_completion_fields(&config.completion)?;
[1006](#1006)
[1007](#1007)    let header = match &config.correlation {
[1008](#1008)        CorrelationStrategy::HeaderName(h) => h.clone(),
[1009](#1009)        CorrelationStrategy::Expression { expr, .. } => expr.clone(),
[1010](#1010)        CorrelationStrategy::Fn(_) => {
[1011](#1011)            return Err(CamelError::RouteError(
[1012](#1012)                "canonical v1 does not support Fn correlation strategy".to_string(),
[1013](#1013)            ));
[1014](#1014)        }
[1015](#1015)    };
[1016](#1016)
[1017](#1017)    let correlation_key = match &config.correlation {
[1018](#1018)        CorrelationStrategy::HeaderName(_) => None,
[1019](#1019)        CorrelationStrategy::Expression { expr, .. } => Some(expr.clone()),
[1020](#1020)        CorrelationStrategy::Fn(_) => unreachable!(),
[1021](#1021)    };
[1022](#1022)
[1023](#1023)    let strategy = match config.strategy {
[1024](#1024)        AggregationStrategy::CollectAll => CanonicalAggregateStrategySpec::CollectAll,
[1025](#1025)        AggregationStrategy::Custom(_) => {
[1026](#1026)            return Err(CamelError::RouteError(
[1027](#1027)                "canonical v1 does not support custom aggregate strategy".to_string(),
[1028](#1028)            ));
[1029](#1029)        }
[1030](#1030)    };

[2255](#2255)    async fn test_set_body_static_processor_works() {
[2256](#2256)        use camel_core::route::{CompiledStep, compose_pipeline};
[2257](#2257)        let def = RouteBuilder::from("t:t")
[2258](#2258)            .route_id("test-route")
[2259](#2259)            .set_body("replaced")
[2260](#2260)            .build()
[2261](#2261)            .unwrap();
[2262](#2262)        let pipeline = compose_pipeline(
[2263](#2263)            def.steps()
[2264](#2264)                .iter()
[2265](#2265)                .filter_map(|s| {
[2266](#2266)                    if let BuilderStep::Processor(p) = s {
[2267](#2267)                        Some(p.clone())
[2268](#2268)                    } else {
[2269](#2269)                        None
[2270](#2270)                    }
[2271](#2271)                })
[2272](#2272)                .map(|p| CompiledStep::Process {
[2273](#2273)                    processor: p,
[2274](#2274)                    body_contract: None,
[2275](#2275)                    lifecycle: None,
[2276](#2276)                })
[2277](#2277)                .collect(),
[2278](#2278)        );
[2279](#2279)        let exchange = Exchange::new(Message::new("original"));
[2280](#2280)        let result = pipeline.oneshot(exchange).await.unwrap();
[2281](#2281)        assert_eq!(result.input.body.as_text(), Some("replaced"));
[2282](#2282)    }

[3394](#3394)        assert_eq!(retry.max_attempts, 5);

Add a step to the catch clause’s sub-pipeline.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/camel_builder/do_try.rs.html#139-142)#### pub fn [on_when](https://docs.rs#method.on_when)(self, predicate: [FilterPredicate](https://docs.rs/camel-api/0.22.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camel_api/filter/type.FilterPredicate.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/camel_builder/do_try.rs.html#139-142)

#### pub fn [on_when](https://docs.rs#method.on_when)(self, predicate: [FilterPredicate](https://docs.rs/camel-api/0.22.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camel_api/filter/type.FilterPredicate.html)) -> Self

Set an additional predicate that must also match for this catch clause to fire.

Sugar for `disposition(ExceptionDisposition::Handled)`.

The caught error is marked handled and the catch clause’s exchange becomes the final result (no re-throw).

Sugar for `disposition(ExceptionDisposition::Propagate)`.

The catch clause runs for side-effects and the original error is re-thrown.

Note: `.continued()` is intentionally NOT provided — Continued is
rejected at parse time for doTry MVP per spec §3 (semantically
ambiguous at catch-clause scope).

# camel_builder::do_try - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/camel-builder/0.22.0/camel_builder/do_try/index.html

## Expand description

Builder types for the `doTry` / `doCatch` / `doFinally` EIP pattern.

These builders provide a fluent API for constructing doTry scopes within a Camel route. Example:

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [DoCatch](https://docs.rs/struct.DoCatchBuilder.html)- Builder
- Builder for a `.do_catch_exception()`/`.do_catch_when()`/`.do_catch_all()`clause.
- [DoFinally](https://docs.rs/struct.DoFinallyBuilder.html)- Builder
- Builder for a `.do_finally()`…`.end_do_finally()`block.
- [DoTry](https://docs.rs/struct.DoTryBuilder.html)- Builder
- Builder for a `.do_try()`…`.end_do_try()`block.

# LoadBalancerBuilder in camel_builder - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/camel-builder/0.22.0/camel_builder/struct.LoadBalancerBuilder.html

`pub struct LoadBalancerBuilder { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Builder for the sub-pipeline within a `.load_balance()` … `.end_load_balance()` block.

Exposes the same step methods as `RouteBuilder` (to, process, filter, etc.)
but NOT `.build()` and NOT `.load_balance()` (no nested load balancers).

Calling `.end_load_balance()` packages the sub-steps into a `BuilderStep::LoadBalance`
and returns the parent `RouteBuilder`.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Set the load balance strategy to weighted selection.

Each endpoint is assigned a weight that determines its probability of being selected.

# MulticastBuilder in camel_builder - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/camel-builder/0.22.0/camel_builder/struct.MulticastBuilder.html

`pub struct MulticastBuilder { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Builder for the sub-pipeline within a `.multicast()` … `.end_multicast()` block.

Exposes the same step methods as `RouteBuilder` (to, process, filter, etc.)
but NOT `.build()` and NOT `.multicast()` (no nested multicasts).

Calling `.end_multicast()` packages the sub-steps into a `BuilderStep::Multicast`
and returns the parent `RouteBuilder`.

#### pub fn [filter](https://docs.rs#method.filter)<F>(self, predicate: F) -> [FilterBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.FilterBuilder.html)

Open a filter scope. Only exchanges matching `predicate` will be processed
by the steps inside the scope. Non-matching exchanges skip the scope entirely
and continue to steps after `.end_filter()`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/camel_builder/lib.rs.html#407-413)#### pub fn [choice](https://docs.rs#method.choice)(self) -> [ChoiceBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.ChoiceBuilder.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/camel_builder/lib.rs.html#407-413)

#### pub fn [choice](https://docs.rs#method.choice)(self) -> [ChoiceBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.ChoiceBuilder.html)

Open a choice scope for content-based routing.

Within the choice, you can define multiple `.when()` clauses and an
optional `.otherwise()` clause. The first matching `when` predicate
determines which sub-pipeline executes.

Add a WireTap step that sends a clone of the exchange to the given endpoint URI (fire-and-forget). The original exchange continues downstream unchanged.

#### pub fn [concurrent](https://docs.rs#method.concurrent)(self, max: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> Self

Override the consumer’s default concurrency model.

When set, the pipeline spawns a task per exchange, processing them
concurrently. `max` limits the number of simultaneously active
pipeline executions (0 = unbounded, channel buffer is backpressure).

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

#### pub fn [sequential](https://docs.rs#method.sequential)(self) -> Self

Force sequential processing, overriding a concurrent-capable consumer.

Useful for HTTP routes that mutate shared state and need ordering guarantees.

Set the route ID for this route.

If not set, the route will be assigned an auto-generated ID.

# SplitBuilder in camel_builder - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/camel-builder/0.22.0/camel_builder/struct.SplitBuilder.html

`pub struct SplitBuilder { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Builder for the sub-pipeline within a `.split()` … `.end_split()` block.

Exposes the same step methods as `RouteBuilder` (to, process, filter, etc.)
but NOT `.build()` and NOT `.split()` (no nested splits).

Calling `.end_split()` packages the sub-steps into a `BuilderStep::Split`
and returns the parent `RouteBuilder`.

# ThrottleBuilder in camel_builder - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/camel-builder/0.22.0/camel_builder/struct.ThrottleBuilder.html

`pub struct ThrottleBuilder { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Builder for the sub-pipeline within a `.throttle()` … `.end_throttle()` block.

Exposes the same step methods as `RouteBuilder` (to, process, filter, etc.)
but NOT `.build()` and NOT `.throttle()` (no nested throttles).

Calling `.end_throttle()` packages the sub-steps into a `BuilderStep::Throttle`
and returns the parent `RouteBuilder`.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/camel_builder/lib.rs.html#1379-1382)#### pub fn [strategy](https://docs.rs#method.strategy)(self, strategy: [ThrottleStrategy](https://docs.rs/camel-api/0.22.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camel_api/throttler/enum.ThrottleStrategy.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/camel_builder/lib.rs.html#1379-1382)

#### pub fn [strategy](https://docs.rs#method.strategy)(self, strategy: [ThrottleStrategy](https://docs.rs/camel-api/0.22.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/camel_api/throttler/enum.ThrottleStrategy.html)) -> Self

Set the throttle strategy. Default is `Delay`.

- `Delay`: Queue messages until capacity available
- `Reject`: Return error immediately when throttled
- `Drop`: Silently discard excess messages

}## Expand description

Shared step-accumulation methods for all builder types.

Implementors provide `steps_mut()` and get step-adding methods for free.
`filter()` and other branching methods are NOT included — they return
different types per builder and stay as per-builder methods.

# cu29 1.0.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cu29/1.0.0

### Why Copper

Already showing up in: ✈️ Flying | 🚗 Driving | 🌊 Swimming | 🚀 Spacefaring | 🤖 Humanoids

### Try Copper In One Click In Your Browser

No setup required. Open one of the live demos in your browser: the simulator runs on the left and the live Copper monitor runs on the right.

These are not mockups: BalanceBot is the exact same application that runs on a Raspberry Pi physical robot, and Flight Controller is the same control stack we run on a microcontroller (STM32H7) on real drones. Copper lets that same graph be recompiled for embedded hardware, a local workstation, or the browser.

Prefer a native app instead of the browser? Install the published demo crates from crates.io:

```
```
The source for the published demo crates above lives in `examples/`.
Cross-framework comparison benchmarks live in `benchmarks/`.

Want to see more Copper in action? Watch the [community showcase video](https://youtu.be/weV_JYaUsmo).

## Get Started

- Requires Rust 1.95 or newer. The latest stable Rust toolchain is recommended.

### Zero To Your First Copper App in 30 Seconds

```
```
`cargo cunew` is the primary Copper bootstrap path. It generates a minimal
source -> task -> sink application. `cargo run` starts the app, prints the
first messages (`Received message: 42`, then `Sink Received message: 43`), and
records to `logs/hello-copper.copper`; stop it with `Ctrl-C` when you've seen
enough. If you have `just` installed, the generated project also includes
helpers like `just log`, `just cl`, and `just resim`. To get situated, open
`copperconfig.ron`, `src/main.rs`, `src/tasks.rs`, and `justfile`.

- Start a new project from templates: [Project Templates](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Project-Templates)
- Browse the live component catalog: [Copper Component Catalog](https://cdn.copper-robotics.com/catalog/index.html)Community components are welcome there too; if you build a reusable Copper component, prefer publishing it as its own crate and adding it to the catalog.
- See a full task graph + runtime walkthrough: [Copper Application Overview](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Copper-Application-Overview)
- Build and deploy an application: [Build and Deploy a Copper Application](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Build-and-Deploy-a-Copper-Application)
- RON configuration reference: [Copper RON Configuration Reference](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Copper-RON-Configuration-Reference)

## Documentation

- Runtime concepts and SDK features: [Copper Runtime Overview](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Copper-Runtime-Overview)
- Task lifecycle: [Task Lifecycle](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Task-Lifecycle)
- Modular configuration: [Modular Configuration](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Modular-Configuration)

- Roadmap: [Roadmap](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Roadmap)

## Python Support

Copper has two very different Python stories:

- Offline Python log analysis: use `cu29-export`and app-specific PyO3 modules in the application crates that expose them. This is a reasonable workflow because Python stays off the runtime hot path.
- Runtime Python task prototyping: use
[components/tasks/cu_python_task](https://docs.rs/components/tasks/cu_python_task)and[examples/cu_python_task_demo](https://docs.rs/examples/cu_python_task_demo). This is for experimentation only and is strongly not recommended for production or realtime robots.

Putting Python inside a Copper task defeats the performance model Copper is built for: it adds allocations, latency, jitter, and middleware overhead, and it ruins the realtime characteristics of the stack. The intended use is to sketch one task in Python, get the behavior right, then rewrite it in Rust.

# cu_bincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cu-bincode/^2.0/

## Expand description

Bincode is a crate for encoding and decoding using a tiny binary serialization strategy. Using it, you can easily go from having an object in memory, quickly serialize it to bytes, and then deserialize it back just as fast!

If you’re coming from bincode 1, check out our [migration guide](https://docs.rs/migration_guide/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Starting from bincode 2, serde is now an optional dependency. If you want to use serde, please enable the `serde` feature. See [Features](https://docs.rs#features) for more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

| Name | Default? | Affects MSRV? | Supported types for Encode/Decode | Enabled methods | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| std | Yes | No | `HashMap`and`HashSet` | `decode_from_std_read`and`encode_into_std_write` | |
| alloc | Yes | No | All common containers in alloc, like `Vec`,`String`,`Box` | `encode_to_vec` | |
| atomic | Yes | No | All `Atomic*`integer types, e.g.`AtomicUsize`, and`AtomicBool` | ||
| derive | Yes | No | Enables the `BorrowDecode`,`Decode`and`Encode`derive macros | ||
| serde | No | Yes (MSRV reliant on serde) | `Compat`and`BorrowCompat`, which will work for all types that implement serde’s traits | serde-specific encode/decode functions in the [serde](https://docs.rs/serde/index.html)module | Note: There are several [known issues](https://docs.rs/serde/index.html#known-issues)when using serde and bincode |

[§](https://docs.rs#which-functions-to-use)Which functions to use

Bincode has a couple of pairs of functions that are used in different situations.

| Situation | Encode | Decode |
|---|---|---|
| You’re working with or`fs::File``net::TcpStream` | `encode_into_std_write` | `decode_from_std_read` |
| you’re working with in-memory buffers | `encode_to_vec` | `decode_from_slice` |
| You want to use a custom [Reader](https://docs.rs/de/read/trait.Reader.html)and[Writer](https://docs.rs/enc/write/trait.Writer.html) | `encode_into_writer` | `decode_from_reader` |
| You’re working with pre-allocated buffers or on embedded targets | `encode_into_slice` | `decode_from_slice` |

**Note:** If you’re using `serde`, use `bincode::serde::...` instead of `bincode::...`

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
let mut slice = [0u8; 100];
// You can encode any type that implements `Encode`.
// You can automatically implement this trait on custom types with the `derive` feature.
let input = (
    0u8,
    10u32,
    10000i128,
    'a',
    [0u8, 1u8, 2u8, 3u8]
);
let length = bincode::encode_into_slice(
    input,
    &mut slice,
    bincode::config::standard()
).unwrap();
let slice = &slice[..length];
println!("Bytes written: {:?}", slice);
// Decoding works the same as encoding.
// The trait used is `Decode`, and can also be automatically implemented with the `derive` feature.
let decoded: (u8, u32, i128, char, [u8; 4]) = bincode::decode_from_slice(slice, bincode::config::standard()).unwrap().0;
assert_eq!(decoded, input);
```

# ctrlc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ctrlc/^3.5/

## Expand description

Cross platform handling of Ctrl-C signals.

[set_handler()](https://docs.rs/fn.set_handler.html) allows setting a handler closure which is executed on
`Ctrl+C`. On Unix, this corresponds to a `SIGINT` signal. On windows, `Ctrl+C` corresponds to
[ CTRL_C_EVENT](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/windows/desktop/ms683242.aspx) or

[.](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/windows/desktop/ms683242.aspx)

`CTRL_BREAK_EVENT`Setting a handler will start a new dedicated signal handling thread where we
execute the handler each time we receive a `Ctrl+C` signal. There can only be
one handler, you would typically set one at the start of your program.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, Ordering};
use std::sync::Arc;
fn main() {
    let running = Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(true));
    let r = running.clone();
    ctrlc::set_handler(move || {
        r.store(false, Ordering::SeqCst);
    }).expect("Error setting Ctrl-C handler");
    println!("Waiting for Ctrl-C...");
    while running.load(Ordering::SeqCst) {}
    println!("Got it! Exiting...");
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#handling-sigterm-and-sighup)Handling SIGTERM and SIGHUP

Handling of `SIGTERM` and `SIGHUP` can be enabled with `termination` feature. If this is enabled,
the handler specified by `set_handler()` will be executed for `SIGINT`, `SIGTERM` and `SIGHUP`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- Ctrl-C error.
- [Signal](https://docs.rs/enum.SignalType.html)- Type
- A cross-platform way to represent Ctrl-C or program termination signal. Other
signals/events are supported via `Other`-variant.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [set_](https://docs.rs/fn.set_handler.html)- handler
- Register signal handler for Ctrl-C.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_set_handler.html)- set_ - handler
- The same as ctrlc::set_handler but errors if a handler already exists for the signal(s).

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Signal](https://docs.rs/type.Signal.html)
- Platform specific signal type

# cu29_runtime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cu29-runtime/^1.0.0/

## Expand description

# Copper Runtime & SDK

[§](https://docs.rs#why-copper)Why Copper

**Rust-first** – ergonomic & safe

**Sub-microsecond latency** – zero-alloc, data-oriented runtime

**Deterministic replay** – every run, bit-for-bit identical

**Interoperable with ROS2** – bridges via Zenoh opening the path for a progressive migration.

**Runs anywhere** – from Linux servers, workstations, SBC to bare-metal MPUs

**Built to ship** – one stack from simulation to production

Already showing up in: ✈️ Flying | 🚗 Driving | 🌊 Swimming | 🚀 Spacefaring | 🤖 Humanoids

[§](https://docs.rs#try-copper-in-one-click-in-your-browser)Try Copper In One Click In Your Browser

No setup required. Open one of the live demos in your browser: the simulator runs on the left and the live Copper monitor runs on the right.

These are not mockups: BalanceBot is the exact same application that runs on a Raspberry Pi physical robot, and Flight Controller is the same control stack we run on a microcontroller (STM32H7) on real drones. Copper lets that same graph be recompiled for embedded hardware, a local workstation, or the browser.

| [

      ](https://cdn.copper-robotics.com/demo/balancebot/index.html)[BalanceBot](https://cdn.copper-robotics.com/demo/balancebot/index.html)Self-balancing robot sim with a live Copper DAG and latency monitor. [Source code](https://docs.rs/examples/cu_rp_balancebot) | [

      ](https://cdn.copper-robotics.com/demo/flight-controller/index.html)[Flight Controller](https://cdn.copper-robotics.com/demo/flight-controller/index.html)Quadcopter flight sim with the same live Copper monitor. [Source code](https://docs.rs/examples/cu_flight_controller) |

Prefer a native app instead of the browser? Install the published demo crates from crates.io:

```
cargo install cu-rp-balancebot
balancebot-sim
cargo install cu-flight-controller
quad-sim
```
The source for the published demo crates above lives in `examples/`.
Cross-framework comparison benchmarks live in `benchmarks/`.

Want to see more Copper in action? Watch the [community showcase video](https://youtu.be/weV_JYaUsmo).

[§](https://docs.rs#get-started)Get Started

- Requires Rust 1.95 or newer. The latest stable Rust toolchain is recommended.

[§](https://docs.rs#zero-to-your-first-copper-app-in-30-seconds)Zero To Your First Copper App in 30 Seconds

```
cargo install cargo-cunew
cargo cunew hello_copper
cd hello_copper
cargo run
```
`cargo cunew` is the primary Copper bootstrap path. It generates a minimal
source -> task -> sink application. `cargo run` starts the app, prints the
first messages (`Received message: 42`, then `Sink Received message: 43`), and
records to `logs/hello-copper.copper`; stop it with `Ctrl-C` when you’ve seen
enough. If you have `just` installed, the generated project also includes
helpers like `just log`, `just cl`, and `just resim`. To get situated, open
`copperconfig.ron`, `src/main.rs`, `src/tasks.rs`, and `justfile`.

- Start a new project from templates: [Project Templates](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Project-Templates)
- Browse the live component catalog: [Copper Component Catalog](https://cdn.copper-robotics.com/catalog/index.html)Community components are welcome there too; if you build a reusable Copper component, prefer publishing it as its own crate and adding it to the catalog.
- See a full task graph + runtime walkthrough: [Copper Application Overview](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Copper-Application-Overview)
- Build and deploy an application: [Build and Deploy a Copper Application](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Build-and-Deploy-a-Copper-Application)
- RON configuration reference: [Copper RON Configuration Reference](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Copper-RON-Configuration-Reference)

[§](https://docs.rs#documentation)Documentation

- Runtime concepts and SDK features: [Copper Runtime Overview](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Copper-Runtime-Overview)
- Task lifecycle: [Task Lifecycle](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Task-Lifecycle)
- Modular configuration: [Modular Configuration](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Modular-Configuration)
- Task automation: [Task Automation with just](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Task-Automation-with-Just)
- Coverage report: [Coverage Report](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/coverage/)
- Supported platforms: [Supported Platforms](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Supported-Platforms)
- Bare-metal development: [Baremetal Development](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Baremetal-Development)
- Component catalog: [Copper Component Catalog](https://cdn.copper-robotics.com/catalog/index.html)
- FAQ: [FAQ](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/FAQ)
- Release notes: [Copper Release Notes](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Copper-Release-Notes)
- Roadmap: [Roadmap](https://copper-project.github.io/copper-rs/Roadmap)

[§](https://docs.rs#python-support)Python Support

Copper has two very different Python stories:

- Offline Python log analysis: use `cu29-export`and app-specific PyO3 modules in the application crates that expose them. This is a reasonable workflow because Python stays off the runtime hot path.
- Runtime Python task prototyping: use
[components/tasks/cu_python_task](https://docs.rs/components/tasks/cu_python_task)and[examples/cu_python_task_demo](https://docs.rs/examples/cu_python_task_demo). This is for experimentation only and is strongly not recommended for production or realtime robots.

Putting Python inside a Copper task defeats the performance model Copper is built for: it adds allocations, latency, jitter, and middleware overhead, and it ruins the realtime characteristics of the stack. The intended use is to sketch one task in Python, get the behavior right, then rewrite it in Rust.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [app](https://docs.rs/app/index.html)
- [config](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)
- This module defines the configuration of the copper runtime. The configuration is a directed graph where nodes are tasks and edges are connections between tasks. The configuration is serialized in the RON format. The configuration is used to generate the runtime code at compile time.
- [context](https://docs.rs/context/index.html)
- User-facing execution context passed to task and bridge process callbacks.
- [copperlist](https://docs.rs/copperlist/index.html)
- CopperList is the main data structure used by Copper to communicate between tasks. It is a queue that can be used to store preallocated messages between tasks in memory order.
- [cuasynctask](https://docs.rs/cuasynctask/index.html)
- [cubridge](https://docs.rs/cubridge/index.html)
- Typed bridge traits and helpers used to connect Copper to external components both as a sink and a source.
- [curuntime](https://docs.rs/curuntime/index.html)
- CuRuntime is the heart of what copper is running on the robot.
It is exposed to the user via the `copper_runtime`macro injecting it as a field in their application struct.
- [cutask](https://docs.rs/cutask/index.html)
- This module contains all the main definition of the traits you need to implement or interact with to create a Copper task.
- [debug](https://docs.rs/debug/index.html)
- CuDebug: lightweight time-travel debugger helpers on top of Copper logs.
- [distributed_](https://docs.rs/distributed_replay/index.html)- replay
- Discovery, validation, planning, and causal execution helpers for distributed deterministic replay.
- [logcodec](https://docs.rs/logcodec/index.html)
- [monitoring](https://docs.rs/monitoring/index.html)
- Some basic internal monitoring tooling Copper uses to monitor itself and the components it runs.
- [payload](https://docs.rs/payload/index.html)
- Copper-friendly payload helpers used in task messages and task-local caches.
- [pool](https://docs.rs/pool/index.html)
- [reflect](https://docs.rs/reflect/index.html)
- Runtime reflection helpers built on top of `bevy_reflect`.
- [replay](https://docs.rs/replay/index.html)
- Shared Clap-backed helpers for replay and resimulation binaries.
- [resource](https://docs.rs/resource/index.html)
- Resource descriptors and utilities to hand resources to tasks and bridges.
User view: in `copperconfig.ron`, map the binding names your tasks/bridges expect to the resources exported by your board bundle. Exclusive things (like a serial port) should be bound once; shared things (like a telemetry bus`Arc`) can be bound to multiple consumers.
- [simulation](https://docs.rs/simulation/index.html)
- `cu29::simulation`Module
- [thread_](https://docs.rs/thread_pool/index.html)- pool
- Construction of configured worker thread pools (std-only).

- [input_](https://docs.rs/macro.input_msg.html)- msg
- [output_](https://docs.rs/macro.output_msg.html)- msg

# cu29_traits - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cu29-traits/^1.0.0/

## Expand description

Common copper traits and types for robotics systems.

This crate is no_std compatible by default. Enable the “std” feature for additional
functionality like implementing `std::error::Error` for `CuError` and the
`new_with_cause` method that accepts types implementing `std::error::Error`.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `std`(default): Enables standard library support- Implements `std::error::Error`for`CuError`
- Adds `CuError::new_with_cause()`method for interop with std error types

- Implements

[§](https://docs.rs#no_std-usage)no_std Usage

To use without the standard library:

```
[dependencies]
cu29-traits = { version = "0.9", default-features = false }
```

# cu29_value - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cu29-value/^1.0.0/

## Expand description

A Copper-oriented value tree used for serialization, logging, and reflection bridges.

The type is a forked/adapted serde-value-style representation with Copper-specific
additions such as [ Value::CuTime](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html#variant.CuTime).

When the `python` feature is enabled, this crate also exposes helpers for converting
between [ Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html) and Python objects through PyO3. Those helpers are used by:

- `cu-python-task`for runtime prototyping across the Rust/Python boundary
- `cu29-export`for offline Python log analysis

The Python bridge is intentionally conservative:

- `None`becomes- `Value::Unit`
- Python lists and tuples become `Value::Seq`
- Python dicts become `Value::Map`
- Python integers are accepted up to the 128-bit range
- Python bytes become `Value::Bytes`

---

# defmt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/defmt/^1.0/

## Expand description

A highly efficient logging framework that targets resource-constrained devices, like microcontrollers.

Check out the defmt book at [https://defmt.ferrous-systems.com](https://defmt.ferrous-systems.com) for more
information about how to use it.

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

The `defmt` wire format might change between minor versions. Attempting to
read a defmt stream with an incompatible version will result in an error,
and any tool used to process that stream should first check for a symbol
named like `_defmt_version_ = X`, where X indicates the wire format version
in use.

Updating your version of defmt might mean you also have to update your
version of `defmt-print` or `defmt-decoder`.
